contributions.text: 6. Whether she plans to provide additional funding for special schools.
contributions.name: Greg Smith

contributions.who: The Minister for School Standards (Georgia Gould)
contributions.text: Special schools are vital for many children with the most complex needs and will remain essential as we bring in SEND reforms. This is why we are investing £3.7 billion of high needs capital funding to create 60,000 specialist places nationwide, with £860 million allocated to councils this year.
contributions.name: Georgia Gould

contributions.text: I appreciate that answer, but the reality is that since taking office, this Government have scrapped plans for a 152-place SEND school in Buckinghamshire. That school would have been no magic bullet and it would not have solved all our problems, but it would have helped the huge number of families that write to me and come to my surgeries desperate to get their children into that specialist support that they need and deserve. It often ends up costing tens of thousands of pounds in taxes to take those children out of county. Will the Minister reconsider the position that the Government have taken on the new school for Buckinghamshire, and give us the school that we need?
contributions.name: Greg Smith

contributions.text: When we looked at the pipeline of some of the later special schools, none of which were funded, we knew that we needed to get more money into the system quicker. My understanding is that the council will have got equivalent money to create specialist places quicker and order to meet the urgent need that we are seeing in communities around the country.
contributions.name: Georgia Gould

contributions.text: Too many young people have been held back by decades of under-investment in specialist provision in my communities, so I was delighted, after our campaigning, to secure a record increase in high needs funding for Hertfordshire council and Central Bedfordshire council, including the biggest increase in the country for Herts. This is already making a difference, with the new SEND unit at Hitchin Boys’ school and the expansion of Ivel Valley school in Biggleswade finally confirmed. We know, though, that we need to go further and that, historically, local authorities have not always done a great job of commissioning the places their communities need, so how will the Department for Education hold both my councils to account to ensure they are doing right by the young people in my community?
contributions.name: Alistair Strathern

contributions.text: We have asked every local authority and integrated care board to develop a SEND reform plan that sets out how they should improve services, including their commissioning, and we will be holding them to account regularly. We are getting quarterly data back from those plans, and in our proposals for the new system we want to develop specialist provision packages, which will be really clear on the specialist provision we expect to see available in every part of the country for the young people who need it.
contributions.name: Georgia Gould

contributions.text: There is huge concern among parents with SEND children that the Government are pressing ahead with their SEND reforms while underdelivering special school places. New modelling that I have seen suggests that 41,600 additional special school places will be needed by the end of the decade. The Minister mentioned 60,000 places, but I am talking only about special school places, not mainstream provision. Will she confirm how many children her analysis shows will need special school places, and how many places the Government expect to deliver, by the end of the decade?
contributions.name: Saqib Bhatti

contributions.text: Our reforms are trying to do two things. First, we are making the mainstream genuinely inclusive; so many children could have thrived in mainstream but are not able to. We are rolling out new teacher training and Experts at Hand, and extra funding is going into mainstream schools to ensure that they are genuinely inclusive. We also recognise that we need new specialist places. The £3.7 billion is to create 60,000 new specialist places, which can be in inclusion bases linked to mainstream schools or in new special schools. We are investing heavily: we are putting £4 billion into early intervention and £3.7 billion into capital. We just did not see that investment under the previous Government.
contributions.name: Georgia Gould
